title: Your First Behavior – Moving an Object
description: Make a GameObject move continuously using transform.Translate and Time.deltaTime.

slides.title: The Transform Component in Code 📐
slides.content:
# Accessing the Transform

Every script attached to a GameObject automatically has a reference to that object's `transform` (lowercase).
- `transform.position` – world position.
- `transform.rotation` – world rotation.
- `transform.localScale` – local scale.
- `transform.Translate(x, y, z)` – moves the object by a given offset.

We'll use `Translate` to create continuous movement.

slides.content: Add this code inside `Update()` to move the object along its forward direction (Z axis) each frame:

quizData.question: What does transform.Translate(0, 0, 1) do?

options.text: Rotates the object around the Z axis
Moves the object 1 unit along its local Z axis
Scales the object by 1 on Z

quizData.explanation: Translate moves the object in the given direction. By default it moves in local space.

slides.title: The Problem with Frame‑Based Movement ⚠️
slides.content:
# Why Speed Varies

If you use `0.1f` per frame, on a 60 FPS machine the object moves 6 units per second. On a 30 FPS machine, only 3 units. That's inconsistent!

We need **time‑based** movement: move at a constant speed regardless of frame rate. Enter `Time.deltaTime`.

slides.title: Time.deltaTime – The Secret Sauce ⏲️

quizData.question: What does Time.deltaTime represent?

options.text: Total time since the game started
The time elapsed between the last frame and the current frame
The time it takes to load the scene

quizData.explanation: deltaTime gives you the time difference, making movements consistent across frame rates.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Local vs World Movement

`Translate` moves in **local space** by default. To move in world space, use `transform.Translate(..., Space.World)`. For moving forward visually (blue arrow), local Z works fine if the object's rotation matches its visual front.
